title: What does a Block say about a callee it could not resolve? Ten grammars for client.send()
brief: `response = client.send(payload)` where `Client = Any`. The analyzer knows the callee's text, the receiver's annotation, the argument's type (from the cable) and the function's declared return. It does not know the parameter's name, the callee's return type, or whether `.id` exists. The screenshot that started this asks whether the word should be `unknown`, `undefined`, `n/a` or `tbd`. Measured first: `undefined` appears 0 times across the 48 boards the corpus ships, and 540 of 1107 ports (48.8%) already carry no type at all. So the real question is not which word — it is which channel, and whether an unresolved slot should look different from the half of the corpus that is merely unannotated. Ten directions, each a real board in the real app.
defaultWhy: Opacity is a property of the call, not of each row, and golden 12's own authored target already says so: “external call · effect unknown”, with the ports carrying only proved types. That is the direction with the fewest invented words and the least ink. It is a fragile lead, though — V10 is two points behind and is not really a rival: it speaks in the silhouette where V4 speaks in the type line, and the two compose. The recommended splice is V4's frame plus V10's view, with V9's inference filling every slot the program proves first, and V1's `Any` as the only word ever written for what is left. `undefined` is not in that set at any weighting: it is a JavaScript value on a board that claims to be a lens over Python.
decisionHinge: The weight on fr4 (spot it without reading). At 15 it is a tiebreak and V4 leads. Raise it to 25 — which is the right call if these boards are read at architecture zoom rather than one call at a time — and V10 wins outright, because a silhouette beats a type line at distance and V4's icon is doing most of that work anyway. The second hinge is whether a partly-resolved call is common: if it is, per-port marking (V5) stops being a schema luxury and the codec gate becomes a cost to pay rather than a reason to stop.
invariants: tldraw stays stock: every direction here rides the Block, port, connection and binding seams that already exist.
The canvas is the program as written; the projection never rewrites the call site to make a nicer picture.
A port is exactly id, name, type, visible, defaultValue, row, branch, and the pyblocks codec narrows it to id, name, type, visible, defaultValue.
A wrong type is worse than no type: the board may be quiet, never mistaken.
`undefined` is not a Python word, not a pyblocks certainty value, and appears nowhere in the committed corpus.
Every capture on this page is the real app rendering a real .systemsketch board, generated through the editor and reopened cold.
boundary: This is a grammar decision with the boards to judge it, not a landed change. No pyblocks projection code, no golden, and no SystemSketch source was modified. The ten boards under sketches/review/ are new files. V5's port dot and V6's authoring loop are drawn with text stand-ins, because neither is expressible in the shipped schema; both are scored on that basis rather than on the stand-in.

requirements.name: A reader can tell what is unknown from what is known
requirements.why: Golden 12 contains both at once. `client` really is annotated `Client`, and `Client = Any` — that is a fact the program states. The callee's parameter name and return type are a different thing: nobody looked. A grammar that spells both the same way loses the only distinction that matters here.
requirements.passCondition: Given the board alone, a reader can say which slots the program declared and which the analyzer failed on.

anchors.3: The distinction exists but needs the inspector or the source to read.
anchors.5: Visible on the Block, from the Block alone.

requirements.name: Every word on the board is a word that already exists
requirements.why: SystemSketch is a lens over Python. `undefined` is a JavaScript value; it is not a Python type, not a pyblocks certainty value (may, must, unknown), and it appears 0 times across the 48 boards the corpus ships. A word invented for the picture is a word the reader has to be taught.
requirements.passCondition: Every token on the Block is either Python source text, a Python type, or vocabulary SystemSketch already ships.

anchors.1: Coins a word from another language.
anchors.3: Reuses a symbol that means something else to a Python reader.
anchors.5: Every token already exists in Python or in the app's own grammar.

requirements.name: Ink is proportional to information
requirements.why: An unresolved third-party call is the least interesting Block on the board — it is where the pipeline stops being yours. It must not shout louder than the four calls that carry the actual work. The corpus already agrees in practice: 540 of 1107 ports (48.8%) carry no type at all and nothing marks them.
requirements.passCondition: Marking the ignorance costs less visual weight than stating a real type.

anchors.1: The unresolved call is the loudest thing on the board.
anchors.5: One mark for the whole call, or none.

requirements.name: You can spot an unresolved call without reading
requirements.why: The reason to draw opacity at all is triage: which parts of this diagram can I trust? That question is asked at board zoom, across dozens of Blocks, not with the cursor on one port row.
requirements.passCondition: The unresolved Block is identifiable in a thumbnail of the board.

anchors.1: Indistinguishable until you zoom in and read.
anchors.3: Visible once you know what to look for.
anchors.5: A different silhouette or colour; obvious at a glance.

requirements.name: Costs no new engine capability
requirements.why: tldraw stays stock and the Block grammar stays closed. A port today is exactly id, name, type, visible, defaultValue, row, branch — and the pyblocks codec narrows that further to id, name, type, visible, defaultValue on the way into the file. A direction that needs a new field spends the budget on a naming question.

variants.name: Any
variants.thesis: Do not invent a word. Python already has a name for a type it cannot narrow, and it is `Any`. Every slot the callee does not fill reads `Any`.
variants.bestWhen: The reader is a Python programmer and you want the board to project straight back to a `.pyi`.
variants.losesWhen: The program genuinely declares `Any` — as golden 12's own `Client = Any` does — and the board can no longer tell the two apart.
keepParts: `Any` as the fallback word when a word must be written
the argument expression as the fallback name
proof: Board: sketches/review/opacity-v1.systemsketch, generated through the editor and cold-reopened.
`Any` is already in the corpus: 6 of 1107 generated ports carry it as a declared type.
Golden 12's own source declares `Client = Any`, which is exactly the collision this direction cannot resolve.

fr1.evidence: `Client` on the receiver row is a declared alias for `Any`; `payload: Any` is an admission of failure. The board writes them the same way.

fr2.evidence: `Any` is `typing.Any`, already imported by the golden's own source.

fr3.evidence: A word in every empty slot: the ignorance costs the same ink as the knowledge.

fr4.evidence: In the scene crop `Any` is the same weight as `bytes`; nothing separates the Block.

g2.evidence: `Any` claims nothing narrower than the truth.

g3.evidence: Title and argument name come from the call site.

variants.name: Question mark
variants.thesis: Keep whatever is known and add one character of doubt. `bytes?` means the cable says bytes and the callee never confirmed it; a bare `?` means nothing is known at all.
variants.bestWhen: Most slots are partly known and you want the partial knowledge on the board rather than thrown away.
variants.losesWhen: The reader knows C#, Kotlin or TypeScript, where `T?` already means `Optional[T]` — a different claim entirely.
keepParts: a suffix rather than a replacement
partial knowledge survives on the row
proof: Board: sketches/review/opacity-v2.systemsketch.
The analyzer's own certainty channel is three-valued (may, must, unknown), so one character cannot carry it — `?` collapses `may` and `unknown`.

fr1.evidence: `bytes?` next to `bytes` is exactly the distinction; it still cannot say a slot is declared `Any`.

fr2.evidence: `?` is not Python. In every language a reader is likely to know it, `T?` means optional.

fr4.evidence: A single glyph at port-label size is invisible in the scene crop.

g2.evidence: The suffix weakens the claim rather than strengthening it.

variants.name: Blank slot
variants.thesis: Draw absence as absence. An unknown type is no text at all — the row carries a name and stops. Anything written there is louder than the information it carries.

variants.name: The frame says it once
variants.thesis: Opacity is a fact about the call, not about each row. The Block's type line says `external · unresolved` once, and every port then carries only what the program actually proves.
variants.bestWhen: The unresolved thing is the callee — which is the usual case, because a third-party object hides its whole signature at once.

the description naming what got absorbed
proof: Board: sketches/review/opacity-v4.systemsketch.

This is already the corpus's authored answer. Golden 12's `target.systemsketch` gives `client.send()` the type line “external call · effect unknown”, a dashed stroke and a grey fill, and describes it as “Receiver resolution, descriptor behaviour, response.id, and side effects are all summarized here”.

The measured gap: that dashed stroke lives in legacy metadata. The native Block has no stroke field — it ships w, h, title, description, blockType, icon, view, views, showDescription, notes, portLayout, expandedWeights, definitionId, definitionKey, draftOrdinal, inputs, outputs — so the type line, description and icon are the whole native voice.

fr1.evidence: `Client` reads as a declaration because nothing contradicts it, and the frame carries the failure. It cannot single out one bad port inside a partly-resolved call.

fr2.evidence: `external · unresolved` is `blockType`, the same field that says `call` and `constructor` everywhere else.

fr3.evidence: One line for the whole call; the port rows are unchanged from a resolved Block.

fr4.evidence: The icon plus the type line are legible in the scene crop; at true board zoom the icon does most of the work.

fr5.evidence: `blockType`, `description` and `icon` are all in BLOCK_SHAPE_PROPS (17 fields), and all survive the codec.

g1.evidence: An ordinary Block with a different type line.

g2.evidence: `bytes` comes from the cable, `str` from run()'s return annotation, `Client` from the parameter annotation.

g4.evidence: All three fields are native and persisted.

variants.name: TODO stub
variants.thesis: An unknown is not a fact, it is a task. Render it as `TODO`, make it clickable, and let the reader type the signature — which is then written out as a `.pyi` stub beside the source.
variants.bestWhen: The unresolved callee is yours, or a dependency you are willing to stub, and the diagram is where you would rather do that work.
variants.losesWhen: The callee is a third-party client you will never annotate — which is exactly golden 12's case.

The corpus's own framing disagrees: golden 12's docstring is “01 plus an object nothing here defines: the boundary must look unknown.” The unknown is the point of the case, not a defect in it.

fr4.evidence: Capitals are spottable in the crop, but they read as a defect rather than a boundary.

fr5.evidence: The text is free; the editing loop and stub writer are new capability.

variants.name: Positional slots
variants.thesis: The name is unknown but the arity and the order are not. Say the true thing: `arg 1` in, `→ 1` out. This is what a decompiler does, and what Nevalang's numbered FanIn slots do.
variants.bestWhen: You want the board to state only facts, and position is the strongest fact left when the signature is gone.
variants.losesWhen: The call used keywords — then position is not just unhelpful, it is wrong.
keepParts: stating arity in the type line
never inventing a name that looks like a real one
proof: Board: sketches/review/opacity-v7.systemsketch.
Prior art already read for this project: Nevalang's `[a, b] -> c` is sugar for a real FanIn node with numbered slots — many-to-one is never a rendering question there.

variants.name: Inferred from the neighbours
variants.thesis: Do not render ignorance — remove it. Propagate types along the cables and back from the function's own return annotation, and most slots fill themselves without ever asking the callee.
variants.bestWhen: The unresolved call sits mid-pipeline, surrounded by resolved neighbours that pin its types from both sides.
variants.losesWhen: The unresolved value is consumed by another unresolved thing — `response.id` is exactly that, and stays unknown.
keepParts: fill every slot the program proves, before writing any placeholder
the description naming where each derived type came from
proof: Board: sketches/review/opacity-v9.systemsketch. The Block carries both derived types and the residue side by side.
Both derivations are sound: the cable that lands on `payload` genuinely carries `bytes`, and `run` genuinely declares `-> str` with `return receipt`.
The residue is the point: `response` is the value `.id` is read from, and nothing in the program constrains it.

fr1.evidence: It shrinks the question rather than answering it; the board still needs a spelling for `response`.

fr2.evidence: Every type shown is a real annotation from the real source.

fr3.evidence: No ink spent on ignorance at all.

fr4.evidence: An inferred board is indistinguishable from a resolved one — which is either the feature or the bug.

fr5.evidence: Needs constraint propagation across the graph, in both directions. Nothing like it exists in the adapter today.

g2.evidence: Only propagates what an annotation or a cable proves; it refuses to guess `response`.
